title: HOW THE COMMERCE OF TOWNS CONTRIBUTED TO THE IMPROVEMENT OF THE COUNTRY.
paragraphs: How the Commerce of Towns Contributed to the Improvement of the Country
The growth and wealth of commercial and manufacturing towns helped improve and cultivate the countryside they belonged to, and they did so in three distinct ways.

First, by providing a large and reliable market for the country's raw produce, towns encouraged farmers to cultivate and improve their land. This benefit was not even limited to the regions where the towns sat; it extended, more or less, to every region the towns traded with. The towns gave all of them a market for some of their raw or manufactured produce, and so gave every one of them some encouragement to work harder and improve. Still, a town's own surrounding country always gained the most from its market, simply because it was nearby. Since the local raw produce cost less to transport, traders could pay growers a better price for it and yet sell it to consumers as cheaply as produce hauled in from farther away.

Second, city dwellers often used the wealth they had earned to buy up any land that came on the market, much of which was frequently uncultivated. Merchants commonly long to become country gentlemen, and when they do, they generally turn out to be the best improvers of all. A merchant is used to putting his money mainly into profitable ventures, whereas a mere country gentleman is used to putting his mainly into spending. The merchant regularly watches his money leave him and come back with a profit; the gentleman, once he has parted with his money, rarely expects to see it again. These different habits naturally shape their temperament and outlook in every kind of business. The merchant is usually a bold investor, the country gentleman a timid one. The merchant is not afraid to commit a large sum all at once to improving his land when he has a fair prospect of raising its value in proportion to the outlay; the gentleman, if he has any capital at all, which is not always the case, rarely dares to use it this way. If he improves at all, he usually does it not with capital but with whatever he can save out of his yearly income. Anyone who has had the chance to live in a trading town set in an undeveloped countryside must often have noticed how much more energetic merchants are in this respect than mere country gentlemen. On top of that, the habits of order, economy, and attention that trade naturally instils in a merchant make him far better suited to carrying out any improvement project profitably and successfully.

Third and finally, commerce and manufactures gradually introduced order and good government, and with them the liberty and security of individuals, among country people who had previously lived almost in a constant state of war with their neighbours and in servile dependence on their superiors. This effect, though it has been the least noticed, is by far the most important of all. Mr Hume is the only writer I know of who has taken any notice of it.

In a country with neither foreign trade nor any of the finer manufactures, a great landowner has nothing to exchange for the bulk of his land's produce beyond what feeds the cultivators, so he consumes the whole surplus in lavish hospitality at home. If that surplus is enough to support a hundred or a thousand men, he can use it in no other way than by supporting a hundred or a thousand men. He is therefore always surrounded by a crowd of retainers and dependants who, having nothing to give in return for their keep but being fed entirely by his bounty, must obey him for the same reason that soldiers must obey the prince who pays them. Before commerce and manufactures spread across Europe, the hospitality of the rich and powerful, from the sovereign down to the smallest baron, surpassed anything we can easily imagine today. Westminster Hall was the dining room of William Rufus, and it may often have been none too large for his company. It counted as a mark of splendour in Thomas Becket that he strewed the floor of his hall with fresh hay or rushes in season, so that the knights and squires who could not find seats would not ruin their fine clothes when they sat on the floor to eat. The great Earl of Warwick is said to have fed 30,000 people every day across his various manors; even if that figure is exaggerated, the real number must have been very large to allow for such an exaggeration. Hospitality of nearly the same kind was still practised not many years ago in many parts of the Scottish Highlands. It seems to be common in every nation that knows little of commerce and manufactures. Doctor Pocock reports that he saw an Arabian chief dine in the streets of a town he had come to in order to sell his cattle, inviting every passer-by, even common beggars, to sit down and share his feast.

The people who occupied the land depended on the great landowner just as completely as his retainers did. Even those who were not actual serfs were tenants-at-will, paying a rent that in no way matched what the land could provide them. A crown, half a crown, a sheep, or a lamb was, some years ago in the Scottish Highlands, a common rent for land that supported a whole family. In some places that is still true today, and money will not buy any more goods there now than elsewhere. In a country where the surplus of a large estate has to be consumed on the estate itself, the owner often finds it more convenient to have part of it consumed away from his own house, provided the people consuming it depend on him as completely as his retainers or household servants do. This spares him the awkwardness of either too large a company or too large a household. A tenant-at-will who holds enough land to feed his family for little more than a token rent depends on the landlord just as fully as any servant or retainer, and must obey him just as unreservedly. Such a landowner feeds his servants and retainers in his own house, and feeds his tenants in theirs. Both draw their subsistence from his bounty, and its continuance hangs on his pleasure.

The power of the ancient barons rested on the authority that great landowners necessarily held, in such conditions, over their tenants and retainers. They inevitably became the judges in peacetime and the leaders in war of everyone who lived on their estates. They could keep order and enforce the law within their own domains, because each of them could rally the whole force of all his people against anyone who committed an injustice. No one else had the authority to do this, the king least of all. In those old times the king was little more than the greatest landowner in his realm, to whom the other great landowners paid certain respects for the sake of common defence against common enemies. For the king to have enforced payment of a small debt within the lands of a great landowner, where all the inhabitants were armed and used to standing by one another, would have cost him, had he tried it on his own authority, almost as much effort as putting down a civil war. He was therefore forced to leave the administration of justice, over most of the country, to those capable of administering it, and for the same reason to leave command of the local militia to those whom the militia would obey.

It is a mistake to suppose that these territorial jurisdictions originated in feudal law. Not only the highest civil and criminal jurisdictions, but also the power to raise troops, to coin money, and even to make by-laws governing their own people, were all rights held outright by the great landowners several centuries before the feudal law was even named in Europe. The authority and jurisdiction of the Saxon lords in England seem to have been as great before the Norman Conquest as that of any Norman lords after it, yet feudal law is not thought to have become the common law of England until after the Conquest. That the great lords in France held the most extensive authority and jurisdictions outright, long before feudal law was introduced there, is a fact beyond doubt. That authority and those jurisdictions all flowed necessarily from the state of property and manners I have just described. Without going back to the remote origins of the French or English monarchies, we can find, in much more recent times, plenty of proof that such effects always follow from such causes. Less than thirty years ago, Mr Cameron of Lochiel, a gentleman of Lochaber in Scotland, used to exercise the highest criminal jurisdiction over his own people without any legal warrant whatsoever; he was not what was then called a lord of regality, nor even a tenant-in-chief, but a vassal of the Duke of Argyll, and not even a justice of the peace. He is said to have done so very fairly, though without any of the usual legal formalities, and it is likely that conditions in that part of the country at the time made it necessary for him to take on this authority in order to keep the peace. That gentleman, whose rent never exceeded £500 a year, led 800 of his own people into the rebellion with him in 1745.

Far from extending the authority of the great allodial lords, the introduction of feudal law can be seen as an attempt to curb it. It set up a regular chain of subordination, with a long train of services and duties running from the king down to the smallest landowner. While a landowner was a minor, his rent and the management of his lands passed to his immediate superior, and so the lands of all the great landowners passed to the king, who took charge of the ward's upkeep and education and, by his authority as guardian, was held to have the right to dispose of the ward in marriage, provided it was to someone suited to his rank. But although this arrangement necessarily tended to strengthen the king's authority and weaken that of the great landowners, it could not do either enough to establish order and good government in the country, because it could not sufficiently alter the state of property and manners from which the disorders sprang. The power of government remained, as before, too weak at the top and too strong in its lesser parts, and the excessive strength of those lesser parts was the very cause of the weakness at the top. Even after feudal subordination was established, the king was as unable as before to restrain the violence of the great lords. They still made war at their own discretion, almost constantly against one another and very often against the king, and the open countryside remained a scene of violence, plunder, and disorder.

But what all the violence of feudal institutions could never achieve, the quiet and imperceptible workings of foreign commerce and manufactures gradually brought about. These slowly gave the great landowners something they could exchange the entire surplus of their lands for and consume themselves, without sharing it with either tenants or retainers. All for ourselves, and nothing for anyone else, seems in every age of the world to have been the base motto of the masters of mankind. So as soon as they found a way to consume the whole value of their rents themselves, they had no inclination to share it with anyone. For a pair of diamond buckles, perhaps, or something equally frivolous and useless, they traded away the maintenance, or what amounts to the same thing, the price of the maintenance, of a thousand men for a year, and with it all the weight and authority that such maintenance gave them. But the buckles were to be entirely their own, with no other human being having any share; whereas under the older way of spending they would have had to share with at least a thousand people. To the men weighing which they preferred, that difference settled everything, and so, to gratify the most childish, mean, and sordid of all vanities, they gradually bartered away their entire power and authority.

In a country with no foreign trade and none of the finer manufactures, a man with £10,000 a year can hardly spend his income on anything other than maintaining, say, a thousand families, all of whom are therefore at his command. In present-day Europe, a man with £10,000 a year can spend his whole income, and generally does, without directly maintaining twenty people or being able to command more than ten footmen who are hardly worth commanding. Indirectly, though, he probably maintains as many people as before, or even more. For although the quantity of luxury goods he exchanges his entire income for is very small, the number of workers employed in producing and preparing those goods must have been very large. Their high price generally comes from the wages of that labour and the profits of all the employers along the way. By paying that price, he indirectly pays all those wages and profits, and so indirectly helps maintain all those workers and their employers. Yet he generally contributes only a very small share to each one: perhaps not a tenth to a very few, not a hundredth to many, and to some not even a thousandth or a ten-thousandth of their whole yearly upkeep. So although he helps maintain them all, they are all more or less independent of him, because they can generally be maintained without him.

When the great landowners spend their rents maintaining their own tenants and retainers, each of them entirely maintains all his own tenants and all his own retainers. But when they spend those rents on tradesmen and craftsmen instead, they may, all of them together, perhaps maintain as many people as before, or even more, given the waste that goes with lavish hospitality. Yet each landowner individually often contributes only a very small share to the upkeep of any one of this larger number. Each tradesman or craftsman draws his living from the custom not of one person but of a hundred or a thousand different customers. So although he is in some measure obliged to them all, he is not absolutely dependent on any single one.

Since the personal spending of the great landowners increased in this way, their number of retainers could not help shrinking just as gradually, until at last the retainers were dismissed altogether. The same cause gradually led the landowners to dismiss the unnecessary part of their tenants too. Farms were enlarged, and the occupiers of land, despite complaints about depopulation, were cut down to the number needed to cultivate it given the imperfect state of farming in those days. By removing the surplus mouths and by demanding the full value of the farm from the tenant, the landowner obtained a larger surplus, or what comes to the same thing, the price of a larger surplus, which the merchants and manufacturers soon gave him a way of spending on himself, just as he had spent the rest. As the cause kept working, he wanted to raise his rents above what his lands, in their actual state of improvement, could afford. His tenants would agree to this only on one condition: that they be secured in their holdings for enough years to recover, with a profit, whatever they spent on further improving the land. The landlord's expensive vanity made him willing to accept this condition, and so long leases came into being.

Even a tenant-at-will who pays the full value of the land is not wholly dependent on the landlord. The money advantages they get from each other are mutual and equal, and such a tenant will risk neither his life nor his fortune in the landlord's service. But a tenant with a long-term lease is entirely independent, and his landlord must not expect from him even the slightest service beyond what is either explicitly written into the lease or imposed on him by the common and known law of the land.

Once the tenants had become independent in this way and the retainers had been dismissed, the great landowners were no longer able to interrupt the regular working of justice or disturb the country's peace. Having sold their birthright, not like Esau for a bowl of stew in a time of hunger and need, but in the recklessness of plenty for trinkets and baubles fitter to be children's toys than the serious pursuits of grown men, they became as insignificant as any solid townsman or tradesman in a city. A regular government was established in the country just as in the town, since nobody now had enough power to disrupt its workings in either place.

It may not bear directly on the present subject, but I cannot help noting that very old families, those who have held a sizeable estate from father to son for many generations in succession, are very rare in commercial countries. By contrast, in countries with little commerce, such as Wales or the Scottish Highlands, they are very common. Arabian histories seem to be full of genealogies, and there is a history written by a Tartar Khan, translated into several European languages, that contains hardly anything else, which proves that ancient families are very common among those nations. In countries where a rich man can spend his income only by maintaining as many people as it will support, he tends to overspend, and his generosity, it seems, is rarely fierce enough to make him try to maintain more than he can afford. But where he can spend the greatest income on himself alone, he often sets no limit on his spending, because he often sets no limit on his vanity or his fondness for himself. In commercial countries, therefore, riches very rarely stay long in the same family, despite the harshest laws aimed at preventing their dispersal. Among simple nations, by contrast, they often do stay, without any laws to that effect; for among shepherd nations like the Tartars and Arabs, the perishable nature of their property makes any such laws impossible.

A revolution of the greatest importance to public happiness was thus brought about by two different groups of people, neither of whom had the slightest intention of serving the public. The great landowners were driven solely by the most childish vanity. The merchants and craftsmen, far less ridiculous, acted purely out of self-interest, pursuing their own shopkeeper's principle of turning a penny wherever a penny was to be had. Neither group had any knowledge or foresight of the great revolution that the folly of the one and the industry of the other were gradually bringing about.

It was in this way that, across most of Europe, the commerce and manufactures of cities, far from being the result of agricultural improvement, became the cause and occasion of the improvement and cultivation of the countryside.

This sequence, however, runs against the natural course of things, and so it is necessarily both slow and uncertain. Compare the slow progress of those European countries whose wealth depends largely on their commerce and manufactures with the rapid advance of our North American colonies, whose wealth rests entirely on agriculture. Across most of Europe the population is not thought to double in less than five hundred years. In several of our North American colonies it is found to double in twenty or twenty-five years. In Europe, the law of primogeniture and various forms of entail prevent the breaking up of great estates and so hinder the multiplication of small landowners. Yet a small landowner who knows every inch of his little property, regards it with all the affection that property, especially small property, naturally inspires, and on that account takes pleasure not just in cultivating it but in adorning it, is generally the most industrious, intelligent, and successful improver of all. Those same laws, besides, keep so much land off the market that there are always more capitals looking to buy than there is land to sell, so whatever is sold always fetches a monopoly price. The rent never covers the interest on the purchase money, and is burdened on top of that with repairs and other occasional charges to which interest on money is not subject. Buying land is, everywhere in Europe, a most unprofitable way to use a small capital. For the sake of greater security, a man of moderate means who retires from business will sometimes choose to put his small capital into land. A professional man, too, whose income comes from another source, often likes to secure his savings the same way. But a young man who, instead of going into trade or a profession, put a capital of two or three thousand pounds into buying and cultivating a small piece of land might indeed expect to live very happily and very independently, but he must say goodbye forever to any hope of great fortune or great distinction, which a different use of his money would have given him the same chance of winning as anyone else. Such a person, moreover, though he cannot aspire to be a great landowner, will often scorn to be a mere farmer. So the small amount of land brought to market, and the high price of what is brought, keeps a great deal of capital from being employed in cultivation and improvement that would otherwise have gone that way. In North America, by contrast, fifty or sixty pounds is often found to be enough capital to start a plantation. There, buying and improving uncultivated land is the most profitable use of the smallest as well as the greatest capital, and the most direct road to all the fortune and distinction the country can offer. Such land in North America can indeed be had almost for nothing, or at a price far below the value of its natural produce, which is impossible in Europe or in any country where all the land has long been private property. If landed estates in Europe were divided equally among all the children whenever a landowner died leaving a large family, the estate would usually be sold. So much land would come to market that it could no longer fetch a monopoly price. The free rent of the land would come no closer to covering the interest on the purchase money, and a small capital could be employed in buying land as profitably as in any other way.

England, thanks to the natural fertility of its soil, the great length of its coastline relative to the size of the whole country, and the many navigable rivers running through it that bring the convenience of water transport even to some of its most inland parts, is perhaps as well suited by nature as any large country in Europe to be a centre of foreign commerce, of manufactures for distant markets, and of all the improvements these can bring. Since the start of Elizabeth's reign, too, the English legislature has been unusually attentive to the interests of commerce and manufactures, and indeed no country in Europe, not even Holland, has laws that are on the whole more favourable to this kind of industry. Commerce and manufactures have accordingly kept advancing throughout this whole period. The cultivation and improvement of the country has no doubt been advancing too, but it seems to have followed slowly and at a distance behind the faster progress of commerce and manufactures. Most of the country had probably already been cultivated before Elizabeth's reign, yet a very large part of it still lies uncultivated, and the cultivation of the far greater part falls well short of what it might be. The law of England, however, favours agriculture not only indirectly, by protecting commerce, but through several direct encouragements as well. Except in times of scarcity, the export of grain is not only free but encouraged with a bounty. In times of moderate plenty, the import of foreign grain is loaded with duties amounting to a ban. The import of live cattle, except from Ireland, is banned at all times, and even from Ireland it was only recently allowed. So those who cultivate the land enjoy a monopoly against their own countrymen in the two greatest and most important products of the land, bread and butcher's meat. Although these encouragements are, at bottom, perhaps entirely illusory, as I shall try to show later, they at least clearly demonstrate the legislature's good intention to favour agriculture. But far more important than any of them, the yeomanry of England are made as secure, independent, and respectable as the law can make them. No country, then, where the right of primogeniture applies, where tithes are paid, and where entails, though against the spirit of the law, are admitted in some cases, can give more encouragement to agriculture than England. And yet this is the state of its cultivation. What would it have been if the law had given no direct encouragement to agriculture beyond what flows indirectly from the progress of commerce, and had left the yeomanry in the same condition as in most other European countries? It is now more than two hundred years since the beginning of Elizabeth's reign, a span as long as human prosperity usually lasts.

France seems to have enjoyed a considerable share of foreign commerce nearly a century before England became known as a commercial country. The French navy was considerable, by the standards of the time, before Charles VIII's expedition to Naples. Yet the cultivation and improvement of France is, on the whole, inferior to England's. The country's law has never given agriculture the same direct encouragement.

The foreign commerce of Spain and Portugal with the rest of Europe, though carried on chiefly in foreign ships, is very considerable. Their trade with their own colonies is carried on in their own ships and is much larger, owing to the great wealth and extent of those colonies. But it has never brought any significant manufactures for distant markets into either country, and most of both still lies uncultivated. Portugal's foreign commerce is older than that of any great country in Europe except Italy.

Italy is the only great country in Europe that seems to have been cultivated and improved in every part through foreign commerce and manufactures for distant markets. Before Charles VIII's invasion, Italy, according to Guicciardini, was cultivated no less in its most mountainous and barren parts than in its flattest and most fertile ones. The country's favourable position, and the large number of independent states then existing within it, probably contributed a good deal to this widespread cultivation. It is also possible, despite this sweeping statement by one of the most judicious and cautious of modern historians, that Italy was not at that time any better cultivated than England is now.

The capital that any country gains through commerce and manufactures is always a very precarious and uncertain possession, until some part of it has been secured and made real in the cultivation and improvement of its land. A merchant, as has rightly been said, is not necessarily the citizen of any particular country. It largely makes no difference to him from what place he carries on his trade, and a very slight annoyance will make him move his capital, and with it all the industry it supports, from one country to another. No part of that capital can be said to belong to any particular country until it has been spread, as it were, over the face of that country, either in buildings or in lasting improvements to the land. No trace now remains of the great wealth said to have been held by most of the Hanse Towns, except in the obscure histories of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. It is even uncertain where some of them stood, or which towns in Europe the Latin names given to some of them refer to. But although the misfortunes of Italy at the end of the fifteenth and the start of the sixteenth centuries greatly reduced the commerce and manufactures of the cities of Lombardy and Tuscany, those regions are still among the most populous and best cultivated in Europe. The civil wars of Flanders, and the Spanish government that followed them, drove away the great commerce of Antwerp, Ghent, and Bruges. Yet Flanders is still one of the richest, best cultivated, and most populous provinces of Europe. The ordinary upheavals of war and government easily dry up the sources of wealth that come from commerce alone. Wealth that comes from the more solid improvements of agriculture is far more durable, and can only be destroyed by those more violent convulsions caused by the depredations of hostile and barbarous nations carried on for a century or two together, like those that happened for a time before and after the fall of the Roman empire in the western provinces of Europe.
Book IV. Of Systems of Political Economy

Political economy, regarded as a branch of the science of a statesman or legislator, sets out two distinct aims: first, to provide a plentiful revenue or subsistence for the people, or more precisely, to enable them to provide such a revenue or subsistence for themselves; and second, to supply the state or commonwealth with revenue enough for public services. It aims to enrich both the people and the sovereign.

The differing pace at which wealth has grown in different ages and nations has given rise to two different systems of political economy for enriching the people. One may be called the system of commerce, the other the system of agriculture. I shall try to explain both as fully and clearly as I can, and I shall begin with the system of commerce. It is the modern system, and is best understood in our own country and our own times.
